questions.q: The Deligne torus $\mathbb{S} = \mathrm{Res}_{\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{G}_m$ has which group of real points?
questions.hint: Weil restriction along $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}$ remembers the multiplicative group of $\mathbb{C}$, viewed as a real algebraic group.
questions.explain: By definition $\mathbb{S}(\mathbb{R}) = \mathbb{G}_m(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{C}^\times$, while $\mathbb{S}(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{C}^\times \times \mathbb{C}^\times$ via the embedding $\mathbb{S}_\mathbb{C} \cong \mathbb{G}_m \times \mathbb{G}_m$. A homomorphism $h\colon\mathbb{S}\to G_\mathbb{R}$ thus packages a real Hodge structure on $\mathfrak{g}$ via $\mathrm{Ad}\circ h$.

questions.q: Which of the following are Deligne's axioms (SV1)–(SV3) for a Shimura datum $(G, X)$?
choices: The Hodge structure $\mathrm{Ad}\circ h$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ has type contained in $\{(-1,1),(0,0),(1,-1)\}$
$G^{\mathrm{ad}}$ has no $\mathbb{Q}$-factor on which $h$ projects trivially
questions.hint: Deligne lists exactly three axioms; one of the choices is a stronger non-required hypothesis.
questions.explain: (SV1)–(SV3) are exactly items 0, 1, 2. Simple connectivity of $G$ is NOT required: $\mathrm{GL}_2$ itself is not simply connected (its derived group $\mathrm{SL}_2$ is), yet it's a perfectly good Shimura datum. (SV2) is what forces $X$ to be a Hermitian symmetric domain.

questions.q: For the Siegel datum $(\mathrm{GSp}_{2g}, \mathfrak{H}_g)$, the complex dimension of the Hermitian symmetric space $\mathfrak{H}_g$ is $\binom{g+1}{2}$. What is this dimension for $g = 4$?
questions.hint: Symmetric $g\times g$ complex matrices have $\binom{g+1}{2}$ independent entries.
questions.explain: $\binom{5}{2} = 10$. So $\mathfrak{H}_4$ has complex dimension $10$; $\mathcal{A}_4$ is a $10$-dimensional Shimura variety, parametrising principally polarised abelian fourfolds.

shim-canonical-model.title: Adelic double quotient and canonical models

questions.q: The Shimura variety at level $K$ is built as the double quotient $\mathrm{Sh}_K(G,X) = G(\mathbb{Q})\backslash X\times G(\mathbb{A}_f)/K$. What replaces this for the classical $G = \mathrm{GL}_2/\mathbb{Q}$ at level $K = K_0(N)$?
questions.hint: Strong approximation collapses the adelic double quotient at level $K_0(N)$ to a single connected arithmetic quotient.
questions.explain: Strong approximation for $\mathrm{SL}_2/\mathbb{Q}$ gives $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f) = \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Q})^+ K_0(N)$ (since $\det K_0(N) = \widehat{\mathbb{Z}}^\times$), so the double quotient reduces to $\Gamma_0(N)\backslash\mathcal{H} = Y_0(N)$. This is the foundational worked example.

questions.q: Which of the following are TRUE about the reflex field $E(G,X)$ of a Shimura datum?
choices: It is the field of definition of the conjugacy class $\{\mu_h\}$ over $\mathbb{C}$
$E(\mathrm{GU}(p,q), \cdot) = K$ for the CM field $K$ defining $G$
questions.hint: Item 1 over-claims; some unitary Shimura data have a non-trivial reflex.
questions.explain: 0, 2, 3 are correct. The reflex $E$ is the smallest number field over which the cocharacter conjugacy class $\{\mu_h\}$ is defined; for $\mathrm{GL}_2$ and $\mathrm{GSp}_{2g}$ it is $\mathbb{Q}$, but for unitary groups defined by a CM field $K$ the reflex is generally $K$ (or its reflex CM field). The canonical model lives over $E$.

questions.q: Order these steps in constructing the canonical model $\mathrm{Sh}_K(G,X)_E$ over the reflex field, from earliest to latest in Deligne's setup.
items: Compute the Hodge cocharacter $\mu_h$ and its reflex field $E = E(G,X)$
Form the complex variety $\mathrm{Sh}_K(G,X)(\mathbb{C}) = G(\mathbb{Q})\backslash X\times G(\mathbb{A}_f)/K$
Use Shimura's reciprocity law on special points to pin down the $E$-rational structure
questions.hint: The reflex is computed before complex points are constructed; descent to $E$ comes last.
questions.explain: Datum first → reflex field next → complex Shimura variety → descent via reciprocity on special (CM) points. Special points are the rigidifiers: the canonical model is uniquely characterised by how Galois acts on them, expressed by the reflex norm.

questions.q: A point $\tau \in \mathfrak{H}_g$ — symmetric $g\times g$ complex matrix with $\mathrm{Im}\,\tau > 0$ — encodes which moduli object?
choices: An elliptic curve with a level-$g$ structure
A principally polarised abelian variety of dimension $g$ (with level structure)
A $g$-dimensional complex torus, no polarisation needed
questions.hint: The positivity of $\mathrm{Im}\,\tau$ is exactly Riemann's bilinear relation for a principal polarisation.
questions.explain: $\tau \in \mathfrak{H}_g$ defines the lattice $\Lambda_\tau = \mathbb{Z}^g + \tau\mathbb{Z}^g \subset \mathbb{C}^g$, the abelian variety $A_\tau = \mathbb{C}^g/\Lambda_\tau$, and a principal polarisation given by the standard symplectic form $E(v_1+\tau v_2, w_1+\tau w_2) = v_1\cdot w_2 - v_2\cdot w_1$. The Torelli theorem says $\tau \bmod \mathrm{Sp}_{2g}(\mathbb{Z})$ is the moduli.

questions.q: What is the complex dimension of $\mathcal{A}_2 = \mathrm{Sp}_4(\mathbb{Z})\backslash\mathfrak{H}_2$, the Siegel modular variety of genus $2$?
questions.explain: $\dim_\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{H}_2 = \binom{3}{2} = 3$. So $\mathcal{A}_2$ is a $3$-dimensional algebraic variety over $\mathbb{Q}$ — the moduli space of principally polarised abelian surfaces. Its $\mathbb{Q}$-points come from genus-$2$ curves (via the Jacobian) or from products of elliptic curves.

questions.q: A student presents the following argument: "Every complex torus $\mathbb{C}^g/\Lambda$ defines a point of $\mathcal{A}_g$." Identify the flawed step.
steps: $\mathbb{C}^g/\Lambda$ is a compact complex Lie group of dimension $g$.
Therefore it is automatically projective algebraic.
Hence it carries a principal polarisation, defining a point of $\mathcal{A}_g$.
questions.hint: For $g \ge 2$, a generic lattice produces a complex torus with NO nonconstant meromorphic functions.
questions.explain: Step 1 is fine — it's just the definition of a complex torus. Step 2 is the false step: a generic $g\ge 2$ complex torus has no nonconstant meromorphic functions and is not algebraic at all. The condition picking out abelian varieties (and Siegel points) is the existence of a positive Riemann form — a polarisation. Step 3 then evaporates because the torus may not have any polarisation, let alone a principal one.

questions.q: Let $F$ be a totally real number field of degree $d = [F:\mathbb{Q}]$ and consider $G = \mathrm{Res}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}\mathrm{GL}_2$. The Hermitian symmetric space attached to this Shimura datum is:
questions.explain: Each real embedding $\sigma$ of $F$ contributes a copy of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$, and hence a copy of $\mathbb{H}^\pm$. So $X = \prod\mathbb{H}^\pm$ and the connected component is $\mathbb{H}^d$. The resulting Hilbert modular variety has complex dimension $d$.

questions.q: Which statements about Shimura curves $X^B$ for a quaternion algebra $B/F$ split at exactly one infinite place are TRUE?
choices: $X^B$ is compact when $B$ is non-split (i.e. $B \ne M_2(F)$)
When $B = M_2(\mathbb{Q})$, $X^B$ specialises to a Hilbert modular surface
Jacquet–Langlands relates $H^1(X^B)$ to a subspace of newforms on the modular curve $X_0(N_B)$
questions.hint: Item 2 confuses dimensions; Shimura curves are always $1$-dimensional.
questions.explain: 0, 1, 3 hold. Item 2 is wrong: when $B = M_2(\mathbb{Q})$ ($F = \mathbb{Q}$), the construction gives back $Y_0(N)$, a modular curve — still $1$-dimensional. Hilbert modular surfaces require $F$ of degree $\ge 2$ AND $B = M_2(F)$ split everywhere. The compactness of non-split $X^B$ (no cusps) makes their cohomology especially clean.

questions.q: For $F = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$ and $G = \mathrm{Res}_{F/\mathbb{Q}}\mathrm{GL}_2$, what is the complex dimension of the resulting Hilbert modular variety?
questions.explain: $[\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5}):\mathbb{Q}] = 2$, so $X = \mathbb{H}^2$ and the Hilbert modular variety is a $2$-dimensional surface — a Hilbert modular surface, parametrising abelian surfaces with real multiplication by $\mathcal{O}_F = \mathbb{Z}[\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}]$. These are the simplest non-classical Shimura varieties beyond modular curves.

questions.q: On the étale cohomology $H^i_{\mathrm{ét}}(\mathrm{Sh}_K\times\overline{E}, \overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell)$, what two algebras act commutingly?
choices: Two copies of the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{E}/E)$
$\mathrm{Gal}(\overline{E}/E)$ and the adelic Hecke algebra of $G$
The adelic Hecke algebra of $G$ and the universal cover deck group
questions.hint: One side is automatic from étale cohomology; the other comes from Hecke correspondences as algebraic cycles on $\mathrm{Sh}_K\times\mathrm{Sh}_K$.
questions.explain: The Galois action is functorial; the Hecke action comes from the moduli interpretation (correspondences $\mathrm{Sh}_K \leftarrow \mathrm{Sh}_{K\cap gKg^{-1}} \to \mathrm{Sh}_K$). They commute because Hecke correspondences are defined over $E$. Eigensystem decomposition under the commutative spherical Hecke algebra produces the Galois representations.

questions.q: For a weight-$2$ newform $f \in S_2(\Gamma_0(N))$ with $T_p$-eigenvalue $a_p$, and $\rho_{f,\ell}\colon \mathrm{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})\to\mathrm{GL}_2(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_\ell)$ the Eichler–Shimura representation, which TRUE for $p \nmid N\ell$?
questions.hint: Modular curves are $1$-dimensional, so the interesting cohomology is in degree $1$, not $2$.
questions.explain: 0–2 are textbook Eichler–Shimura. Item 3 is wrong: $X_0(N)$ is a curve (dimension $1$), so the Galois rep lives in $H^1_{\mathrm{ét}}$, not $H^2$. Higher-weight cusp forms appear in higher étale cohomology of the universal elliptic curve over $X_0(N)$ (Deligne's construction).

questions.q: Match each constructor of automorphic Galois representations to the Shimura-variety setting they used.
right: Higher-weight cusp forms via étale sheaves on the universal elliptic curve
Shimura curves over totally real $F$, Hilbert modular forms
Siegel and unitary Shimura varieties via the stable trace formula
questions.hint: Match historical generality: from $\mathrm{GL}_2/\mathbb{Q}$ weight $2$ outward.
questions.explain: Eichler–Shimura: $X_0(N)$ + $\mathrm{GL}_2/\mathbb{Q}$ weight 2. Deligne: extends to higher weights via universal elliptic curve. Carayol: Hilbert/quaternionic via Shimura curves over totally real $F$. Kottwitz / Brylinski–Labesse (and many others): Siegel + unitary Shimura varieties, requiring the stable trace formula and the Langlands–Kottwitz method of §6.

questions.q: Honda–Tate theory classifies isogeny classes of abelian varieties over $\mathbb{F}_q$ by what kind of algebraic numbers?
choices: Weil $q$-numbers — algebraic integers all of whose archimedean conjugates have absolute value $\sqrt{q}$
questions.hint: The condition that picks them out is the Weil bound: Frobenius eigenvalues on $H^1$ have absolute value $\sqrt{q}$.
questions.explain: Weil $q$-numbers are algebraic integers $\pi$ with $|\sigma(\pi)| = \sqrt{q}$ for every embedding $\sigma$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Honda–Tate (1969) bijects these (modulo conjugation) with $\mathbb{F}_q$-isogeny classes of abelian varieties. The classification feeds directly into the Langlands–Kottwitz formula.

questions.q: What does the Langlands–Kottwitz formula relate?
choices: Twisted orbital integrals on the Hecke side, after stabilization
The Hodge–Tate weights of the Galois representation
questions.hint: It's a point-counting/trace formula identity, not a Hodge-theoretic or volume statement.
questions.explain: $|\mathrm{Sh}_K(\mathbb{F}_q)| = \sum c(\gamma_0;\gamma,\delta)\,\mathrm{O}_\gamma(\mathbf{1}_K^p)\,\mathrm{TO}_\delta(\phi_p)$. After Kottwitz stabilization, comparing with the Arthur–Selberg trace formula on the automorphic side gives local-global compatibility. Hodge–Tate weights are fixed by the cocharacter $\mu_h$ (§1) and aren't an output of Langlands–Kottwitz.

questions.q: If $|X_0(11)(\mathbb{F}_p)| = p + 1 - a_p$ and $a_2 = -2$ for the modular elliptic curve $E_{11}$, what is $|X_0(11)(\mathbb{F}_2)|$?
questions.explain: $|X_0(11)(\mathbb{F}_2)| = 2 + 1 - (-2) = 5$. The Eichler–Shimura side identifies $a_p$ with the trace of $\mathrm{Frob}_p$ on $\rho_{11}$ and with the $T_p$-eigenvalue of the unique normalised newform of level $11$; Langlands–Kottwitz at $p = 2$ recovers exactly this count from the geometric side.
